query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build platform to around 500 °C during the additive manufacturing process of HEAs reduces thermal gradients, thereby minimizing residual stresses and cracking, which in turn improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built high-entropy alloy components produced under standard SLM/DED conditions without build platform preheating, which typically exhibit significant thermal gradients, residual stress accumulation, microcracks, and dimensional distortions.
generation.intervention: Implement controlled build platform preheating to approximately 500 °C during the additive manufacturing process.
generation.conditions: This intervention is applied during SLM or DED processing of high-entropy alloys using similar powder feedstocks and energy input parameters, with all other process variables held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform temperature field leads to moderated cooling rates, reduced thermal gradients, and lower residual stress; as a result, the microstructure forms with fewer defects (e.g., crack initiation sites) and more uniform grain/cell boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By preheating the build platform, the temperature differential between deposited material and substrate is reduced. This diminishes shrinkage, warpage and the localized high cooling rates that normally create stress concentrations and microcrack formation, thereby enhancing the dimensional precision and mechanical performance of the fabricated parts.
generation.predicted_outcome: Parts produced with platform preheating will show reduced warpage and microcrack density, improved dimensional accuracy, and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and better integrity) relative to parts made without preheating.
generation.baseline: Components fabricated under standard conditions without substrate preheating, which commonly exhibit higher thermal gradients, residual stresses, dimensional distortions, and fabrication-induced defects.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy alloy systems processed by SLM/DED under comparable energy density and processing parameters; variations in alloy composition, machine configuration, or deposition method might alter the effectiveness of the preheating intervention.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements (e.g., percentage reduction in defects or increase in mechanical strength) are uncertain and may depend on specific machine settings, material composition, and exact temperature control during processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA specimens using an identical SLM or DED process: one set with the build platform preheated to 500 °C and a control set without preheating. Ensure all other process parameters (laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, etc.) remain constant. Post-process both sets identically, and then measure dimensional accuracy, residual stress, microstructural defect density, and mechanical properties.
measurements: Quantitative dimensional analysis (e.g., warpage, shrinkage measurements)
Residual stress mapping (using X-ray diffraction or other stress measurement techniques)
Microstructural characterization (via SEM or optical microscopy to assess crack or defect density)
Mechanical tests (tensile, compression tests to benchmark yield and ultimate strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in dimensional distortions and defect density, along with an improvement in mechanical properties compared to the controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Despite using maximal attainable laser power output of 500 W and the mentioned thermally insulated platform, there is still a notable amount of undissolved Nb and Zr particles present in the microstructure. Nonetheless, their presence highlights a remaining challenge in achieving complete melting of elemental powders in L-DED []. Interestingly, while undissolved particles were still present, their detrimental effect on compressive yield strength appears to be low. The compression yield strength achieved in the studied material is comparable to that of the equimolar CrNbTiZr alloy that was subjected to hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C and 207 MPa for 1 h, followed by a 24 h annealing at 1200 °C [,,,]. This resemblance in properties is important, since achieving such mechanical properties directly from the additive manufacturing process, without requiring further heat treatments or HIP, offers considerable benefits in terms of cost and time savings. The occurrence of undissolved particles might potentially be reduced by lowering the scanning velocity as reported in [], or by incorporating additional remelting steps []. cited_evidence.text: Microsections were prepared and throughout the initial investigation, samples with noteworthy lack of fusion defects or significant keyhole porosity were ruled out. In addition to these defects, large horizontal cracks were seen as critical defects, disrupting the fabrication process due to the deterioration of the thermal conductivity towards the substrate plate, as well as the possible detachment of entire sections. Therefore, the initial set of 16 samples was reduced to four samples, which exhibited large defect-free sections, and the defects present were predominantly limited to vertical cracking (Figure 6). Vertical cracks were expected due to the absence of preheating (substrate plate preheating was not employed), coupled with the larger than usual layer thickness. Raising the build space temperature to lower cooling rates and thermal gradients is the most common approach to minimize cracking. New research also suggests that high-frequency laser power modulation is a suitable approach to prevent cracking [].
